HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e114.summary: Title rubric for the third question of the Prologue: whether evident knowledge of the objects of faith can be communicated to a wayfarer.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e125.summary: States the question: whether certain science and evident knowledge of what the Catholic faith holds can be communicated by divine power to a wayfarer who remains strictly within the limits of the wayfaring state.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e141.summary: Principal argument for the affirmative: a power can attain whatever falls under its adequate object; everything faith holds falls under the adequate object of our intellect, since the possible intellect can become all things (De anima 3) and every truth and entity seems comprehended under its object, including the truth expressed by the articles.
claims: A power can attain whatever falls under its adequate object.
The possible intellect can become all things, so the truths of faith fall under its adequate object.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e171.summary: Argument to the contrary: what truly beatifies is not communicable to a wayfarer, since the blessed cannot be a wayfarer; evident knowledge of the Trinity truly beatifies, as Augustine says the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are what make us blessed, and John 17:3 identifies eternal life with knowing God.
claims: What truly beatifies cannot be given to a wayfarer.
Evident knowledge of the Trinity is beatifying.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e199.summary: Divides the question into four articles: what the question asks; whether true faith can remain together with such perfect knowledge, in this life or the next; whether faith and opinion are compossible about the same thing; and, to understand the first article, what the adequate object of our intellect is.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e217.summary: Editorial 'Resolutio': the doctor's chief conclusion is that God by his absolute power can communicate to a wayfarer every truth the blessed see in the divine essence without placing him outside the limits of the wayfaring state.
claims: By absolute power God can communicate to a wayfarer every truth seen by the blessed without removing him from the wayfaring state.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e230.summary: Article heading: Article 1, on what the question asks.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e237.summary: Thomas takes the affirmative, on the ground that where divine power is concerned — wonderful, incomprehensible and infinite — we should extend rather than restrict it wherever no contradiction is implied.
claims: Divine power should be extended rather than restricted wherever no contradiction is involved.
concepts: non-contradiction as limit of divine power

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e261.summary: First argument: God can reveal scientifically and evidently to a wayfarer, who remains a wayfarer, everything the blessed see in the divine essence; so he can give evident knowledge of the articles. Proof of the first part: as God stands to prime matter (pure potency among sensibles), able to induce any form including those to which it is only in obediential potency, so he stands to our intellect (pure potency among intelligibles); our intellect is in obediential potency to the truths of faith, else it could not see them even in beatitude.
claims: God can induce in the intellect any intelligible form, including those to which it is in obediential potency, as he can in prime matter.
The intellect is in obediential potency to the truths of faith.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e327.summary: Proof of the second part (that such a person remains a wayfarer): one remains a wayfarer so long as one is neither damned, blessed, nor destined to purgatory. Such a person need not be damned (he could have charity), need not be blessed (God could suspend the will's act, without which there is no fruition, while preserving the intellect's act, the intellect being naturally prior to the will), and need not be in purgatory (he could have so much grace that nothing remains to purge).
claims: A wayfarer is one who is neither damned, blessed, nor in purgatory.
God can suspend the will's act of fruition while conserving the intellect's vision.
Without the will's fruition one is not blessed.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e364.summary: Second argument: if such evident knowledge were impossible, the impossibility would stem from God, from the nature of our intellect, from the intellect's indisposition, or from the incompatibility of faith and evident science. Not from God, for nothing is impossible with him; not from the intellect's nature, for then it would be impossible in every state, as for a horse or ass; not from indisposition, for God can instantly induce any disposition, even the light of glory.
claims: No impossibility arises from God, from the nature of the intellect, or from its indisposition.
God can instantly infuse any disposition the intellect is capable of, including the light of glory.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e397.summary: Reply to the objection that such a person would then be blessed: if God infused the light of glory while wholly suspending the will's act, the person would remain a wayfarer, since vision does not beatify without the will's complacency. Nor does the fourth option hold, since (Article 2) faith and clear knowledge are compatible.
claims: Vision without the will's complacency does not beatify.
Faith and clear knowledge are compatible.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e419.summary: Introduces a certain doctor (Scotus) who argues for the same conclusion but posits many things as doubtful as the conclusion itself or more so; Thomas will summarize his reasoning.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e432.summary: The doctor's argument: whoever can be given perfect quidditative knowledge of a subject under its proper ratio can know scientifically all truths virtually contained in it (Grosseteste); perfect knowledge of deity under its proper ratio is communicable to a wayfarer; so all truths of faith — those about the possible depending on God's free choice and those that hold of God intrinsically, like the Trinity — can be manifested. For the minor he distinguishes (Quodlibet) abstractive cognition, of an object whether existing or not, present or not, from intuitive cognition, of an existing and present thing as such; only intuitive is beatific, so a wayfarer can receive abstractive but not intuitive knowledge of deity. That God can be known abstractively is argued: whatever God does by means of his essence he can do immediately by his will alone; he moves the blessed to intuition by his essence as present; so by will alone he can cause a clear, naked but abstractive knowledge of his essence, since the will is the first and universal cause and the essence as object is a quasi-contracted, secondary cause.
claims: Perfect quidditative knowledge of a subject yields knowledge of all truths virtually contained in it.
Abstractive cognition is indifferent to the existence and presence of its object; intuitive cognition is of the existing, present object as such.
Only intuitive cognition of God is beatific, so abstractive knowledge of the divine essence could be given to a wayfarer.
Whatever God does by his essence as object he can do by his will alone.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e539.summary: Further arguments by others for abstractive knowledge of God: God can cause without our will the same assent to the articles he now causes through it, since what a first cause can do with a secondary cause it can do without it; but an assent not from the inclining will must come from evidence of the thing, not intuitive (not communicable to a wayfarer), hence abstractive.
claims: An assent to the articles caused without the will would have to arise from evidence, which could only be abstractive for a wayfarer.
concepts: role of the will in faith

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e562.summary: Another argument: whatever has being and essence conceptually distinct can have its essence known abstractively; in God being and essence differ conceptually, since the divine essence can be conceived without truth, goodness or any other attribute, and thus without being.
claims: Where essence and existence are conceptually distinct, the essence can be known abstractively.
God's essence can be conceived without his being.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e580.summary: Another argument: deity can be conceived without its presence to us, which is a relation of reason, and the divine essence can be conceived without any relation of reason; therefore abstractively.
claims: Presence is only a relation of reason, so God can be conceived without it, i.e., abstractively.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e596.summary: Another argument: the divine essence is no less knowable to us than a creature's; a rose is knowable both intuitively and abstractively; so too God.
claims: God is no less knowable than a rose, which can be known abstractively.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e607.summary: Another argument: what is prior in understanding can be separated from everything posterior, and the divine essence is prior in understanding to being and every attribute.
claims: The divine essence, prior in understanding to its being, can be conceived apart from it.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e618.summary: Another argument: wherever memory remains from a prior intuitive act, abstractive cognition of the same object can exist; Paul remembered being rapt to the third heaven (2 Cor 12), which Augustine interprets as the naked deity.
claims: Memory of an intuition is abstractive cognition of its object.
Paul remembered his vision of the divine essence, so he had abstractive knowledge of it.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e645.summary: Another argument: by the same kind of knowledge by which one knows an act and its relation to an object one can know the object; the beatific act and its relation to the beatific object, being creatures, can be revealed abstractively to a wayfarer; so too the divine essence.
claims: One can know an object by the same kind of cognition as its act and relation; the beatific act can be known abstractively, so the divine essence can as well.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e666.summary: Thomas states these do not conclude and lays out his plan: first solve these reasons; second bring arguments against them; third show how adherents of that opinion answer those arguments and refute their answers; fourth posit two conclusions directly contradicting the doctor's two conclusions.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e686.summary: Thomas accepts the doctor's conclusion and principal reason but denies his qualification of the minor, that the knowledge communicable to a wayfarer can only be abstractive and not intuitive.
claims: The communicated knowledge need not be merely abstractive.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e704.summary: Reply to the first argument (whatever God does by his essence he can do by will alone): the major is false, since by the same reasoning whatever God does by his power he could do by will alone without power, which is contradictory; the divine will has no more priority to the essence than to the power or any attribute.
claims: The divine will is not prior to the essence any more than to power or other attributes.
The argument would absurdly imply God could act without his power.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e728.summary: Second objection to that major: since the divine essence is an infinite sea (Damascene), it is unintelligible that will or any attribute be prior to it; no attribute has infinite power except by identity with the essence, which is formally infinite (as shown in q.1); otherwise it would be infinite wherever found, even in creatures.
claims: Attributes have infinite power only through identity with the formally infinite essence.
No attribute is prior to the divine essence.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e754.summary: Third objection: as finite will is to infinite will, so finite essence is to infinite essence; permuting, as finite will is to finite essence so infinite will is to infinite essence; but a finite will cannot do without its essence what it does by means of it.
claims: By proportion, the infinite will can no more act without the infinite essence than a finite will without its essence.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e774.summary: Fourth objection: such a power would belong to the divine will either as will (then to every will) or as divine (then it is really identical to the essence and cannot be prescinded from it in any real action).
claims: The divine will, being really identical with the essence, cannot act apart from it.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e791.summary: Fifth objection: the will has all its activity from the essence rather than vice versa, since the essence is formally first and purest act, and the first in any genus causes the rest, really where things differ really and conceptually where they differ conceptually.
claims: The essence, as purest act, is the source of the will's activity, not vice versa.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e809.summary: Sixth objection: things distinguished by reason keep the same order they have where distinguished really; where will differs really from essence, it has no priority to it, but the reverse; so too where they differ only in reason. An objection is raised that these arguments concern the essence absolutely, not as object, where it has a contracted ratio.
claims: Conceptual order mirrors real order, and will is posterior to essence in creatures.
Objection: the essence as object has a contracted ratio.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e833.summary: Reply: the divine essence is most truly object to the divine intellect, yet not contracted but taken most absolutely; any contraction or precision of it relative to a created intellect is not due to its being an object but to the one to whom it is objected.
claims: Contraction of the divine essence as object arises from the created intellect, not from the essence's being an object.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e857.summary: Reply to the second argument (assent without the will): granted the premises, it follows only that God can cause without our will the same kind of adhesion he now causes through it, which is not from clear knowledge. The divine will can incline our intellect no less than our will can, so such adhesion would come from divine inclination, not from the evidence of the thing.
claims: God can cause the assent of faith by directly inclining the intellect, without evidence.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e883.summary: Reply to the third argument (conceptual distinction of essence and existence): if the conceptual difference arises from an intrinsic difference in the thing, as in a rose, the major holds; if it arises from a defect in the conceiver, abstractive knowledge of such an essence would be greatly diminished, not perfect. The distinction in God arises from the conceiver's defect, since whoever conceived God perfectly would conceive his essence and being in one concept.
claims: A conceptual distinction rooted in the knower's defect yields only diminished knowledge.
A perfect conception of God grasps essence and existence in a single concept.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e916.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: the antecedent is false for perfect conception, since what is known must be present to the intellect in itself or in a likeness, and no creature can perfectly represent the divine essence; so if it is perfectly known it must be actually present — call that presence a relation of reason or what you will. Imperfectly, however, the divine essence can be known in a created likeness, in the way...
claims: What is known must be present in itself or in a likeness.
No creature perfectly represents the divine essence, so perfect knowledge of it requires its actual presence.
God can be imperfectly known through created likenesses.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e941.summary: Completes the preceding reply with Romans 1:20: the invisible things of God are seen through the things that are made.
claims: God is imperfectly known through creatures, as Romans 1:20 states.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e952.summary: Reply to the fifth argument (God as knowable as a rose): the major is false, since our intellect is to what is most manifest in nature as the owl's eye to the sun; unless God shows himself intuitively, he is known less perfectly than a rose, because a rose can have a representative for abstractive cognition, while the divine essence, owing to its infinite and unlimited perfection, cannot.
claims: Unless God shows himself intuitively, he is known less perfectly than a rose.
The divine essence, being infinite, cannot have an adequate representative for abstractive cognition.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e976.summary: Reply to the sixth argument (priority of essence in understanding): it tells against the opponent, whose earlier argument assumed the essence as object is posterior to the will, while here he says it is prior to every attribute, the will included — a contradiction. In any case, such priority exists only for a deficient intellect, not for one knowing God perfectly.
claims: The opponent contradicts himself on the priority of essence and will.
Priorities among divine rationes exist only for a deficient intellect.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e998.summary: Reply to the seventh argument (Paul's memory): imperfect knowledge remained in Paul, as Augustine shows on 1 Cor 13:12 ('now I know in part'), saying that Paul too knew obscurely; and Paul said this after his rapture, which on the opponent's own view occurred at his conversion.
claims: Paul's memory of his rapture left him only imperfect knowledge of God.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1030.summary: Reply to the eighth argument: the major is false, since acts and relations, being created and finite, can be perfectly represented abstractively in a created likeness, whereas the infinite divine essence cannot; nor does perfect knowledge of an effect lead to quidditative knowledge of the cause unless the effect is adequate to it. All these reasons thus either conclude nothing about abstractive knowledge of the divine essence or show only that it can be imperfectly known through creaturely likenesses.
claims: Created acts can be represented abstractively, but the infinite essence cannot.
Only an adequate effect leads to quidditative knowledge of its cause.
Abstractive knowledge of God through likenesses is always imperfect.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1056.summary: Transitional: having dealt with these arguments, Thomas will now argue against the supposedly perfect abstractive knowledge of the divine essence, beginning with the major of their reasoning.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1077.summary: First counter-argument: if the divine will can immediately do whatever God does in us through his essence, then since God causes intuitive knowledge through his essence, the will could cause intuition without the essence — which would be intuitive and not intuitive, since intuition (on their view) terminates at the essence as existing and present.
claims: The opponents' principle implies an intuition without the presence of its object, a contradiction.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1097.summary: Second counter-argument: abstractive knowledge of God is either more perfect, equally perfect, or less perfect than intuitive. Not the first two, for then it would beatify as intuitive does, which they deny; not the third, for then God, who knows creatures abstractively before they exist and intuitively after, would progress from imperfect to perfect knowledge as things come into being, which is impossible.
claims: If abstractive knowledge were less perfect than intuitive, God's knowledge would grow as creatures come to be.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1121.summary: Third counter-argument: when two cognitions concern the same object under the same ratio and are both naked and perfect, if one is beatific so is the other; abstractive and intuitive are such on the opponents' view.
claims: Two equally naked and perfect cognitions of the same object must both beatify or neither.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1134.summary: Fourth counter-argument: a mere relation of reason added to a cognition cannot make it beatific unless it is beatific already; but on their view presence (a relation of reason) added to abstractive cognition makes it intuitive; so if abstractive is not beatific, neither is intuitive.
claims: A relation of reason cannot make a non-beatific cognition beatific.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1152.summary: Fifth counter-argument: what includes existence in its quidditative concept cannot be conceived abstractively, since abstractive cognition abstracts from existence and non-existence; God, as supremely necessary being, cannot be conceived as not existing.
claims: God's essence includes existence and so cannot be conceived abstractively.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1170.summary: Sixth counter-argument: all abstractive cognition presupposes intuitive cognition, as induction shows — God knows his essence intuitively before (in reason) knowing things to be made abstractively; angels know themselves intuitively before others abstractively; in humans and beasts, sensory intuition precedes abstraction — but on their view a wayfarer cannot know God intuitively, hence not abstractively.
claims: Abstractive cognition always presupposes intuitive cognition.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1197.summary: Seventh counter-argument: whatever a wayfarer knows abstractively is abstracted from a phantasm, but there can be no phantasm of the divine essence.
claims: Wayfarers abstract from phantasms, and there is no phantasm of God.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1208.summary: A certain doctor's response to the first counter-argument: the principle says 'whatever' God can do through the essence, not 'every relational thing'; intuitive cognition necessarily includes a relation to the object's actuality, which God cannot make without the presence of its term — as he cannot make a son without a father — while abstractive cognition includes no such relation.
claims: Intuitive cognition includes a relation to the object's actuality and so requires the object's presence; abstractive does not.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1234.summary: Thomas rejects this: every cognition relates to its object as measured to measure and so includes a real relation to the object (Metaph. 5), so neither abstractive nor intuitive cognition can be absolved from it. Moreover, the doctor's own words elsewhere destroy the response, since he argues that intuitive cognition in its absolute entity is formally independent and really distinct from its relation to the object, so they can be separated by divine power.
claims: Every cognition is really related to its object as the measured to its measure.
The doctor elsewhere holds that intuitive cognition is separable from its relation to the object, contradicting this reply.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1284.summary: The doctor's response to the second counter-argument: intuitive cognition is the less noble; and God had intuitive knowledge of non-existent things from eternity.
claims: God knows non-existent things intuitively from eternity.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1295.summary: Thomas replies that this contradicts the very doctor being defended, who rightly holds that intuitive cognition is of the present as present and the existing as existing, whereas creatures did not exist from eternity.
claims: Intuitive cognition is of the existing as existing, so God could not know non-existent creatures intuitively from eternity.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1308.summary: The doctor's response to the third: though both cognitions are of the same object, they do not bear on it uniformly, so one may beatify without the other. Thomas answers that this does not help, since the opinion defended holds that by both the object is perfectly and openly known, so if the object makes one beatific it makes the other so too.
claims: If both cognitions perfectly and openly know the object, both would be beatific.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1331.summary: The doctor's response to the fourth: the relation of presence does not beatify; the divine essence grasped in the noblest mode of knowing does.
claims: The divine essence known in the noblest mode beatifies, not the relation of presence.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1342.summary: Thomas replies that just as the relation does not beatify, neither does the mode, but the divine essence itself; so the same argument applies to the mode as to the relation.
claims: Neither a relation nor a mode beatifies, but only the divine essence.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1353.summary: The doctor's first response to the fifth counter-argument: God's essence and existence differ conceptually. Thomas notes he has already refuted this.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1364.summary: Further rebuttal: conceiving the divine essence one conceives it either as wholly necessary being, in which case existence belongs to its intrinsic concept and they do not differ conceptually, or as possible being, which is false and contrary to philosophy and theology. The doctor's second response is that God's existence and actuality can be known quasi-imaginatively and abstractively.
claims: Conceiving God as necessary being includes existence in his concept.
Conceiving God as merely possible is false.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1386.summary: Reply to the second response: as an essence joined to existence exists, so an essence known with its existence is known as existing; and intuitive cognition is of the existing as existing, so the posited abstractive cognition would be intuitive.
claims: Knowing an essence together with its existence is intuitive cognition.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1402.summary: The doctor's response to the sixth counter-argument: this abstractive cognition is not acquired through intuition but created by God in the intellect.
claims: Abstractive cognition of God could be directly created by God without prior intuition.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1412.summary: Thomas, though placing little weight on that counter-argument, challenges the response: even if God creates such knowledge, it must terminate at and be specified by its object; either it terminates at the divine essence through some created medium (and is imperfect, since no created medium contains the essence perfectly) or immediately (and is intuitive). Positing abstractive cognition thus necessarily posits intuitive.
claims: Cognition of God either terminates through a created medium, and is imperfect, or immediately, and is intuitive.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1436.summary: The doctor answers the seventh counter-argument as he did the eighth, so it can be refuted in the same way.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1445.summary: Thomas posits his two promised conclusions: first, perfect intuitive knowledge of the divine essence is communicable by God's power to a wayfarer; second, perfect abstractive knowledge of the divine essence cannot be communicated to a wayfarer or anyone else. The first conclusion is directly supported by the two reasons given at the opening of the article.
claims: Perfect intuitive knowledge of the divine essence can be communicated to a wayfarer by divine power.
Perfect abstractive knowledge of the divine essence cannot be communicated to anyone.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1467.summary: Further argument for the first conclusion: by absolute power a damned soul remaining damned can see God's essence intuitively, so a fortiori a wayfarer remaining a wayfarer can. The damned can see God because the natural gifts of Lucifer and his companions remain intact (Augustine), God is intimately present to every creature, and as first agent he can supply or dispense with any disposition — he could make the owl see the sun more clearly than an eagle. Such a one need not be blessed, since no one is blessed without charity, which only God creates and which he is not compelled to create by acting on the intellect.
claims: By absolute power God could show his essence intuitively to a damned spirit who remains damned.
No one is blessed without charity, which God need not infuse.
If even the damned could see God, a fortiori a wayfarer could.
concepts: vision of God by the damned

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1546.summary: Anticipated objection: it does not follow that one not blessed remains damned, since he could remain a wayfarer, intermediate between damned and blessed.
claims: A non-blessed person could be a wayfarer rather than damned.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1557.summary: Reply: as God is not compelled to give charity, so he is not compelled to give time for repentance; so if he is not blessed he remains damned. The same argument applies to a sinful wayfarer, and so much more can God do this in a just wayfarer's intellect.
claims: God need not grant time for repentance, so the damned who sees God but is not blessed remains damned.
A fortiori God can give intuitive vision to a just wayfarer.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1576.summary: Further argument: there is no reason to deny God can work such wonders in spiritual nature rather than corporeal, since an intellectual soul perfected by grace and charity has a greater inclination to the intuitive vision of God than bodies have to what miracles have wrought in them — e.g., Lot's wife turned into salt (Gen 19) or scattered dust reassembled into human bodies at the resurrection.
claims: If God works miracles in bodies with no natural aptitude, he can a fortiori grant the vision of God to a soul inclined to it by grace.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1613.summary: Further argument: Christ was a true wayfarer yet never ceased to see the divine essence intuitively.
claims: Christ was both a wayfarer and a seer of God.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1624.summary: Anticipated objection: Christ was also truly blessed. Thomas replies that he was blessed whenever he willed, but not always, for had he continuously remained in beatific fruition he would have felt no pain — as even a drop of spiritual joy made martyrs like Lawrence on the gridiron think little of their torments. Thomas says this only disputatively, perhaps holding the opposite in Book 3, d.15.
claims: Christ was blessed whenever he willed, but not continuously, else he would not have suffered.
This is held only disputatively, with a possible retraction in Book 3.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1659.summary: Patristic authority for the first conclusion: Ambrose on Luke 1 says God is seen if he wills and not seen if he does not; Augustine, De videndo Deo, endorses this, saying God is invisible by nature but seen when and as he wills — showing Augustine holds Thomas's view.
claims: God is invisible by nature but seen when and as he wills.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1721.summary: Further argument: an accident depends on substance in being and acting no less than the intellect depends on the will; but by God's power accidents are separated from substance in being and acting, as in the Eucharist, where accidents without a subject retain all their operations; therefore the intellect can have perfect operation without the will's operation, and thus without beatitude.
claims: If accidents can act without their substance in the Eucharist, the intellect can act without the will.
The intellect is naturally prior to the will, since the known good is the will's object.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1758.summary: Thomas notes that this seems to conflict with 'our venerable doctor' (Giles of Rome), who holds it impossible for the intellect to see the divine essence openly without the will loving, since the will's intention is required in the intellect's act for three reasons.
claims: Giles of Rome holds that open vision of God without the will's love is impossible.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1775.summary: Giles's first reason: without the will's intention the intellect could be turned away from the object.
claims: The will's intention keeps the intellect fixed on its object.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1784.summary: Giles's second reason: although many species are in the intellect, none moves it to its act unless through the will's intention we are borne onto the phantasms, since a species by itself lacks enough actuality to cause understanding.
claims: Intelligible species need the will's intention to cause actual understanding.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1802.summary: Giles's third reason: intention is required for ordered judgment; as light can impress on a sleeper's eye without judgment, so an impression of the divine essence could be conserved in the intellect without the will's intention, but no judgment could arise from it without that intention.
claims: Judgment from an impression requires the will's intention.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1824.summary: With reverence for Giles, Thomas says he does not understand this: God can supply any genus of cause except material and inherent formal causes insofar as they involve imperfection; the will's intention is neither the material cause of understanding nor inherent in the intellect, being an act elicited by the will, so whatever it causes in the intellect it causes efficiently, and God can supply it most perfectly.
claims: God can supply any efficient cause.
The will's intention acts on the intellect only as an efficient cause and can therefore be supplied by God.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1857.summary: Reply to Giles's first reason: God can fix the power on its object more perfectly than any intention of the will.
claims: God can hold the intellect to its object better than the will can.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1868.summary: Reply to Giles's second and third reasons: even on Giles's view God is not understood through a species, and in any case God could cause greater actuality in a species than the will's intention could; God could even annihilate will and intellect, preserve the soul's essence, and cooperate with it for perfect operation. Giles's remark that if impression sufficed the air would see fails, since air has no visual power; Giles himself says the impression of the species in the pupil is really vision. Moreover, since the will is borne only to what is known, there must be real understanding from the object's impression before the will elicits its intention.
claims: God can supply whatever actuality the will's intention would provide.
Impression in a cognitive power is cognition.
The will is borne only to what is already known, so understanding precedes the will's intention.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e1939.summary: Another doctor argues in support of Giles: if fruition could be removed while open vision remained, the presence of the enjoyable object to the will would be removed while vision remains, which is impossible since the object is present to the will only through vision; nor can the will simply be suspended from its act, since the act results from the proportion between power and object, which must first be dissolved. Thomas replies that divine power is no less efficacious than created power, and created power can suspend a power from its act in the object's presence — e.g., through figures, characters and words, someone standing before another's open eyes may not be seen, though still colored and tangible.
claims: Some argue fruition cannot be removed while vision remains.
Created powers can suspend a faculty's act in the presence of its object, so divine power can too.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2004.summary: Second example: setting aside practices the Church forbids more because of human wickedness than intrinsic evil, there is a stone that renders a person touching it invisible to those present, without removing color or anything from the object, as shown by visibility returning when the stone is set down; so the stone suspends the observers' visual power. Thomas will not shorten the hand of the Most High by denying God what the least creatures can do.
claims: A natural stone can suspend the power of sight in the presence of its object.
God can do whatever lesser creatures can do in suspending a power.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2048.summary: Third example: the deeds of Alexander describe a small stone that, uncovered, outweighed any quantity of gold on a balance. Since gold is the heaviest metal tending downward, yet its tendency is suspended with no resistant medium, why could God not suspend the will's tendency toward a present object? This is not attraction like a magnet's, since the stone's pan descends and the gold's rises; nor superior weight, since covered with earth the stone ceases to suspend the gold's descent.
claims: Alexander's stone suspends gold's natural tendency without attraction or superior weight.
So God can suspend the will's tendency toward a present object.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2133.summary: Fourth example: a glorified body present to someone is sometimes seen and sometimes not, without losing its color; this is a suspension of visual power, as is clear when the same body is seen by one person and not another equally present. Further, Luke 24: the disciples' eyes were held so they did not recognize him.
claims: Glorified bodies can be seen by one and not another equally present, showing suspension of sight.
The Emmaus disciples' eyes were held from recognizing Christ.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2164.summary: Further scriptural examples: the Sodomites struck with blindness so they could not find the door (Gen 19), blind only to the door; Balaam's ass saw the angel while Balaam did not, and later Balaam saw it while his servants did not (Num 22); Christ suspended the sight of those wishing to stone him in the Temple and passed through those wishing to throw him from the cliff.
claims: Scripture records God's selective suspension of sight in the presence of its object.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2199.summary: Conclusion from these examples: by divine power a creature's power can be suspended from its act however present its object; so the consequence and its proof used by that doctor fail, and the instance is answered, since God can suspend a power without dissolving the proportion of object to power. Thomas concludes that by divine power clear, intuitive knowledge of the divine essence can be produced in a wayfarer's intellect, with the will suspended from all acts toward that object, and he would remain a wayfarer, since only perfect beatitude removes one from the wayfaring state and true beatitude requires the will's act of fruition, which is clinging to something with love for its own sake (Augustine).
claims: God can suspend a power without dissolving its proportion to the object.
A wayfarer can have intuitive vision of God with the will suspended and remain a wayfarer.
Beatitude consists essentially in fruition, an act of the will.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2259.summary: Second argument that such a person is not blessed: all delight in any power arises from the will's complacency as well as from the power's act, without which nothing is delightful; with the will suspended there is no complacency and so no beatific fruition, which includes love and delight in its definition.
claims: All delight arises from the will's complacency.
Without the will's act, there can be no beatific fruition.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2277.summary: Third argument: even if God did not suspend the will but left it in its natural state and did not create charity and grace, a person with intuitive vision would still remain a wayfarer, having beatitude only as the philosophers posited it — union with separate substances through the intellect's perfect act — which would not remove anyone from the way, since on the will's side there would only be natural love.
claims: Intuitive vision without charity gives only philosophical beatitude, which does not end the wayfaring state.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2312.summary: Objections against the conclusion: what distinguishes the state of the way from that of the fatherland is not communicable to the wayfarer, and intuitive vision of God is such (1 Cor 13:12, 'now through a glass darkly, then face to face').
claims: Intuitive vision of God distinguishes the fatherland from the way and so cannot be given to a wayfarer.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2330.summary: Second objection: what cannot be communicated to the damned without contradiction is what the punishment of loss intrinsically excludes; the punishment of loss is commonly defined as the lack of the vision of God.
claims: The pain of loss is defined as the lack of the divine vision, so the damned cannot have it.
concepts: vision of God by the damned

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2348.summary: Third objection: Fulgentius says God's face is so glorious that if the damned saw it they would feel no pain.
claims: If the damned saw God they would feel no pain.
concepts: vision of God by the damned

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2359.summary: Reply in general: all such statements are to be understood according to God's ordained power, not his absolute power. Specifically to the first: the distinction between way and fatherland lies not in vision alone but more in the consummate love or fruition consequent on it (Augustine: full joy is to enjoy the Trinity; Ps 35:9–10).
claims: Such authorities concern God's ordained, not absolute, power.
The way and the fatherland are distinguished chiefly by fruition, not vision alone.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2409.summary: Reply to the second: the punishment of loss is called lack of the divine vision because, under God's ordained power, lacking the vision necessarily entails lacking beatific fruition, in which the punishment of loss principally consists, just as eternal beatitude principally consists in its possession.
claims: The pain of loss consists principally in the lack of fruition.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2427.summary: Reply to Fulgentius: it is compatible that one feel no pain (and so not suffer the punishment of sense) yet remain damned by the punishment of loss, lacking fruition through suspension of the will. Statements that a damned soul shown God's face would be blessed mean that God would not suspend the will but infuse charity, so that by absolute power the damned would become blessed — which no Catholic would deny.
claims: One can lack the pain of sense yet suffer the pain of loss.
By absolute power God could make a damned soul blessed by infusing charity.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2463.summary: Proof of the second conclusion (perfect abstractive knowledge of God is impossible): it would bear on the essence either immediately (and so be intuitive) or through a medium. A medium that is itself known must either virtually contain or be adequate to what is known through it, and no created thing can contain or equal the divine essence. A medium that is only a ratio cognoscendi (species) is also impossible: such a medium is needed only to supply an absent object, but God is more intimate to each thing than it is to itself (Augustine); the medium must be more spiritual than its object, but nothing is more spiritual than God; and a species would not make the cognition abstractive anyway, since knowledge by species is abstractive only insofar as the essence can be abstracted from its existence, which is impossible for God.
claims: Perfect abstractive knowledge of God is impossible.
No created medium contains or equals the divine essence.
A species is needed only for an absent object, and God is always intimately present.
Cognition through a species is not abstractive unless the essence can be abstracted from existence, which is impossible for God.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2567.summary: Thomas rejects some followers of Scotus who say abstractive cognition bears immediately on the naked divine essence in order to save their master's intent, since Scotus himself (Quodlibet) says the beatific act cannot be abstractive, as that could exist whether the object existed or not, and that abstractive cognition attains the object not in itself but in a participated likeness. Thus Scotus posits abstractive cognition through a created medium, and it follows against him that it is not quidditative and perfect, for philosophers and theologians distinguish adequate and inadequate effects...
claims: Scotus himself holds that abstractive cognition attains its object in a participated likeness.
Followers of Scotus who claim immediate abstractive cognition of God contradict their master.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2615.summary: Completes the argument: an adequate effect leads to knowledge of what the cause is, but an inadequate effect leads only to knowledge that it is; since no creatable thing can equal the divine essence, abstractive knowledge can never be quidditative and perfect with respect to it.
claims: Only an adequate effect yields quid est knowledge of its cause.
No creature is adequate to God, so abstractive knowledge of God cannot be quidditative.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2633.summary: Article heading and question: whether the habit of infused faith and the intuitive knowledge of the fatherland can remain together.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2645.summary: Thomas answers Article 2 affirmatively: the habit of infused faith and intuitive knowledge of the fatherland can coexist.
claims: Infused faith and intuitive vision can coexist.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2656.summary: Argument: faith and clear vision are no less compatible than the light of faith and the light of glory, since when antecedents are compatible so are their consequents; clear vision follows the light of glory, and the habit of faith is the light of faith or follows from it. That the two lights are compatible is then proved.
claims: If the light of faith and the light of glory are compatible, so are faith and vision.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2676.summary: Proof that the lights are compatible: things having neither material nor formal repugnance are compossible. The two lights lack material repugnance, unlike two whitenesses in one subject, since they differ in species; and they lack formal repugnance, since they are not contradictory or privative (both are positive), not contrary (light is contrary to darkness, not light — faith's contrary is unbelief), and not relatively opposed (relatives are simultaneous by nature, but faith precedes glory).
claims: The lights of faith and glory differ in species and so have no material repugnance.
They are opposed in none of the four modes of opposition, and so have no formal repugnance.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2720.summary: Objection: faith and science cannot coexist, so neither can faith and clear vision. Arguments for the antecedent: evident and non-evident contradict, and science involves evidence while faith involves inevidence; faith and opinion cannot coexist (opinion adheres with fear, faith firmly), so neither faith and science; 'possible not to assent' and 'not possible not to assent' contradict, and the believer can withhold assent while the knower cannot; no mean is compatible with an extreme in its perfection, and faith is a mean between science and opinion (Hugh of St. Victor); accidents ordered to opposites, as faith and science to seeing obscurely and clearly, are incompatible.
claims: Evidence and inevidence contradict.
Faith and opinion are incompatible.
The believer can dissent, the knower cannot.
Faith is a mean between science and opinion and cannot coexist with an extreme.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2804.summary: Further arguments: the same power cannot be perfect and imperfect regarding the same object, and faith's knowledge is imperfect while science's is perfect; and just as one part of the eye cannot have dispositions to see the same object clearly (eagle) and obscurely (owl), so neither can the intellect.
claims: One power cannot be both perfect and imperfect concerning the same object.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2826.summary: Further arguments: faith makes one adhere to credibles 'only' because of the speaker's authority, and 'only' excludes all other adhesion; perfect and imperfect in the same genus cannot coexist, and science and faith are distinguished as perfect and imperfect assent; and one intellect cannot be inclined to the same object by diverse inclinations one of which is simply perfect, as one mobile cannot be inclined to one term by diverse inclinations unless each is imperfect, and a demonstratio potissima would empty all others.
claims: Faith adheres only on authority, excluding other adhesion.
Perfect and imperfect assent cannot coexist.
A perfect inclination excludes others to the same term.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e2884.summary: Eleventh argument: as opinion stands to fear so faith stands to enigma; since fear is intrinsic to opinion, enigma is intrinsic to faith. Thomas rejects these and argues for compatibility: abstractive and intuitive cognition of the same created object coexist in an angel (who keeps abstractive knowledge of an eclipse after seeing it, else he would forget), and the repugnance between evident and non-evident is no greater than between present and non-present; so faith and science can coexist. A certain doctor also argues that the formal rationes of faith (assent on authority) and science (assent by demonstration) are compossible: one who believes an astronomer that the moon is smaller than the earth and later sees it by the eclipse does not lose but strengthens his faith; demonstration preceding or following authority confirms rather than removes the assent.
claims: Abstractive and intuitive cognition of the same object coexist in angels.
The repugnance between evident and inevident is no greater than between present and absent.
Assent from authority and assent from demonstration are compossible and mutually confirming.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3008.summary: Further argument for compatibility: Aristotle and other doctors, Catholic and philosophical, often adduce authorities after demonstrating a conclusion, which would be pointless unless faith from authority could coexist with evident science; otherwise authority would either destroy the demonstrated assent or produce nothing.
claims: Adducing authority after demonstration presupposes that faith and science can coexist.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3032.summary: Reply to the first argument: for contradiction it is not enough that terms concern the same thing; they must be taken in the same respect. Evident according to science contradicts non-evident according to science, but not inevident according to faith. Also the minor is false, since one with certain science can still firmly adhere by faith to the authority he previously believed; so inevidence is not so intrinsic to faith as to exclude science's evidence.
claims: Contradiction requires the same respect, not merely the same object.
Inevidence is not so intrinsic to faith as to exclude scientific evidence.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3069.summary: Reply to the second argument: Thomas denies that faith and opinion cannot coexist. Opinion, with respect to its imperfection, cannot coexist with faith, but in the substance of the habit it can (Topics 4: faith is vehement opinion). Fear is not of opinion's essence, since the stronger opinion grows the less fear there is; Boethius calls an argument 'a reason producing belief about a doubtful matter'. Opinion even confirms faith: one seeing Christ raise the dead has a probable argument that he is God and cannot lie, confirming the Trinitarian article. Opinion as judging that things could be otherwise is incompatible with faith and science; as concluding through a probable middle term without attending to whether things could be otherwise, it is compatible with both — else Aristotle would vainly add probable reasons to necessary ones.
claims: Opinion in its substance, without imperfection, can coexist with faith.
Fear is not of the essence of opinion.
Opinion can confirm faith.
Opinion taken as probable inference without regard to contingency coexists with faith and science.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3141.summary: Reply to the third argument: 'possible not to assent' and 'not possible not to assent' contradict only if taken according to the same habit.
claims: Modal contradiction of assent holds only within the same habit.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3152.summary: Reply to the fourth argument begins: there are two kinds of mean, one virtually participating in both extremes, as red between white and black...
claims: A mean may virtually participate in both extremes.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3164.summary: ...and the other a mean broadly speaking, agreeing with one extreme in one respect and with the other in another — as quantity between substance and quality (able to underlie quality when separated by divine power, but inhering like quality), or demonstratio quia between probable syllogism and propter quid demonstration. Of the second kind the major (a mean excludes extremes) is false; faith is a mean between science and opinion only in the second sense.
claims: A mean broadly speaking does not exclude the extremes.
Faith is a mean between science and opinion only in the broad sense.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3201.summary: Anticipated objection: the same reply could be made to the second argument against Henry (q.2 a.1) about the intermediate light of theology.
claims: Thomas's reply about faith as mean could rescue Henry's intermediate light.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3212.summary: Reply: Henry's mean is a mean of the first kind, by composition or participation, as his dawn example shows, where the mean increases toward one extreme as it decreases toward the other; but here faith's approach to science does not weaken opinion but strengthens it.
claims: Henry's intermediate light is a mean by participation, unlike faith's relation to science and opinion.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3236.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: the minor is false; seeing clearly and obscurely are opposed within the same genus of cognition but not across different genera, as clear knowledge of things in the Word and obscure knowledge in their own genus do not conflict.
claims: Clear and obscure seeing conflict only within the same genus of cognition.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3256.summary: Reply to the sixth argument: one subject can be perfect and imperfect according to diverse accidents, as an apple perfectly red and imperfectly sweet; and the intellect can be called perfect by both faith and science, each perfecting in its own way.
claims: One subject can be perfect and imperfect in different respects.
Faith and science each perfect the intellect in their own mode.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3278.summary: Reply to the seventh argument: the eye analogy fails because those ocular dispositions would be of the same species and thus materially repugnant, unlike faith and science.
claims: Faith and science differ in species and so lack material repugnance.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3295.summary: Reply to the eighth argument: 'only' can qualify faith — faith of itself causes assent only through authority (somewhat true) — or the believer — the believer can adhere only through authority (false).
claims: Faith of itself assents through authority, but the believer may also adhere through other means.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3313.summary: Reply to the ninth argument: the major is false, since red and sweet share a proximate genus yet one thing can be perfectly red and imperfectly sweet; if 'same genus' means same species, the minor is false, since assent of faith and assent of science differ in species as faith and science do, there being no greater difference in causes than in effects among things per se ordered.
claims: The assent of faith and the assent of science differ in species.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3335.summary: Reply to the tenth argument: the consequent is not false, and both proofs assume falsehoods. A mobile can have perfect and imperfect inclinations to the same term, as lead is perfectly inclined downward by its weight but imperfectly by a broad shape that slows its motion. And one thing can be both cause and caused (Physics 2), so even if demonstrated a priori as caused, it can be demonstrated a posteriori as cause; denying this would be ignorance of the Posterior Analytics.
claims: A body can have perfect and imperfect inclinations to the same term.
A thing demonstrated a priori can also be demonstrated a posteriori.
concepts: a priori vs a posteriori demonstration

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3381.summary: Reply to the eleventh argument: the minor fails in three ways, the first being that fear is not of opinion's intrinsic ratio; opinion is distinguished from science not by fear, nor faith by inevidence, but by their sources: science by necessary reason, opinion by probable reason, faith by authority.
claims: Science, opinion and faith are distinguished by their grounds: necessary reason, probable reason and authority.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3401.summary: The second and third failures: when opinion increases, fear decreases; and opinion is a positive habit whereas fear is privative.
claims: Fear decreases as opinion increases.
Opinion is positive, fear privative.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3412.summary: Notes that those who see these three instances, some of whom hold the reasoning just mentioned, try to remove them as best they can.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3424.summary: Their answer to the first instance: adhesion through a probable middle term is necessarily uncertain and fearful. Thomas rejects this: fear is in the opining intellect not from probability but from lack of a habit (science or faith) causing firm adhesion; so fear is not intrinsic to opinion and does not follow from it per se but from the privation of firm habits — as shown by the fact that without any opinion one would fear no less, lacking such habits, and that when those habits are present fear disappears though opinion remains.
claims: Fear arises from lack of firm habits, not from the probability of opinion.
When science or faith are present, fear is removed while opinion remains.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3481.summary: Their answer to the second instance: the increase of opinion with decreasing fear belongs to opinion not as opinion but as a way to science or faith.
claims: Opinion's growth reducing fear belongs to it as a way to science.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3494.summary: Thomas accepts this with an addition: just as diminished fear belongs to opinion as a way to science, so does great fear or any fear — great fear as a long way, slight fear as a short way. Hence no fear is essential to opinion as such.
claims: All degrees of fear belong to opinion as a way to science, not as opinion, so fear is not essential to opinion.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3520.summary: Their answer to the third instance: it arises from the false imagining that fear is a privation annexed to opinion and enigma to faith; rather, fear is opinion itself, a fearful habit, and enigma faith itself. Otherwise the light of faith could pass from enigmatic to clear and become the light of glory, and vice versa, since a subject can pass from privation to habit.
claims: Fear and enigma are not privations annexed to opinion and faith but identical with them.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3551.summary: Thomas rejects this: the privation is founded not in the light of faith but in the intellect of the believer, so it does not follow that the light of faith becomes the light of glory or vice versa; rather, God giving open vision removes that darkness from the intellect, and if he removed the light of glory the intellect would again be subject to it, the light of glory remaining substantially unchanged.
claims: The privation of enigma is founded in the intellect, not in the light of faith.
The light of glory removes the intellect's darkness without changing the light of faith.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3580.summary: Introduces patristic authorities that seem opposed to the conclusion: Augustine, 'faith is believing what you do not see'; Gregory, 'faith has no merit where human reason provides proof'; Hebrews 11:1 with the gloss that of things seen there is not faith but knowledge (Thomas the apostle saw a man and believed God); and 1 Cor 13, 'when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away.'
claims: Several authorities seem to make faith incompatible with vision or knowledge.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3625.summary: Reply to Augustine: he means that we can have true faith in this life without open vision, not that faith cannot coexist with a habit of science through which, though not through faith, the intellect can elicit clear vision.
claims: Augustine's definition concerns faith without vision, not the incompatibility of faith with science.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3647.summary: Reply to Gregory: in the fatherland we do not merit. Reply to Hebrews and the gloss: they speak of faith as it is de facto in the wayfarer, not as it is in the comprehensor or possibly in the wayfarer; if clear vision were given to a wayfarer by absolute power, he would not necessarily lose the habit of faith, as neither do the blessed.
claims: There is no merit in the fatherland.
The authorities speak of faith de facto in wayfarers, not of what is possible by absolute power.
The blessed retain the habit of faith.
concepts: habit of faith in the blessed

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3673.summary: Reply of some to 1 Cor 13: faith is done away as to its imperfection but remains as to its substance and perfection.
claims: Faith is removed only as to its imperfection.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3684.summary: Thomas objects that unless more is said, faith would be done away no more than charity, since charity too loses its wayfaring imperfections (tepidity, lack of fervor) in the fatherland.
claims: Removal of imperfection alone does not distinguish the evacuation of faith from that of charity.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3700.summary: Thomas's answer: faith is done away differently from charity; faith ceases as to the act of believing but not as to the habit, while charity ceases neither in act nor in habit.
claims: In heaven faith ceases in act but not in habit; charity ceases in neither.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3713.summary: Anticipated objection: a habit never actualized would be posited in vain.
claims: A habit never exercised would be pointless.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3723.summary: Reply: it is not in vain, since it adorns and perfects the soul, as many things in the glorified body are for beauty rather than function; every habit of the holy soul is an adornment, as the blessed soul after resurrection will have temperance and fortitude without their operations. Alternatively, if believing acts could occur in heaven, faith's greater evacuation would concern the necessity of the act, not the act itself, as created science (evening knowledge) remains in heaven though 'knowledge will be destroyed' as to necessity. Thomas adds that he says this hypothetically, since it is now not permitted because of Pope Benedict's new constitution (Benedictus Deus), which states that vision and fruition of the divine essence do away with acts of faith and hope as theological virtues in the blessed.
claims: Unexercised habits in heaven adorn the soul.
Faith's evacuation may concern the necessity of its act rather than the act itself.
Benedict XII's constitution forbids holding that acts of faith and hope remain in the blessed.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3802.summary: Article heading and question: whether faith and opinion are compossible concerning the same object.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3811.summary: Thomas passes over Article 3, since Article 2 sufficiently showed how faith and opinion can coexist; it may also be treated in Book 3 when discussing the habit of understanding.
claims: The compatibility of faith and opinion was already shown in Article 2.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3829.summary: Article heading and question: what the adequate object of our intellect is.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3838.summary: Thomas distinguishes two capacities of the intellect and two corresponding adequate objects. According to its natural capacity, free of any supernatural influence, its adequate object is 'phantasiable being', immediately (what falls under a phantasm) or mediately (what can be inferred from such knowledge). According to its obediential capacity — what it can receive without contradiction with God's supernatural cooperation — its adequate object is being as being, taken universally to include creature and creator, created and creatable.
claims: The adequate object of the intellect by natural capacity is phantasiable being, immediate or mediate.
The adequate object by obediential capacity is being as being, including God.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3901.summary: Proof of the first conclusion: the adequate object of the intellect's natural capacity includes everything the intellect can naturally know and nothing it cannot. Phantasiable being does so, since nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses, mediately or immediately, and all such is knowable by the intellect (De anima 3).
claims: Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.
Phantasiable being is coextensive with what the intellect can naturally know.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3938.summary: Proof of the second conclusion: the adequate object of the intellect's obediential capacity includes all that God can reveal to it, and being as being does so, since God can reveal himself (as shown and as faith holds), and so much more any created or creatable being; the intellect is in obediential potency to know God by essence, and so a fortiori to every being.
claims: God can reveal himself and therefore any created or creatable being to the intellect.
Being as being is the adequate object of the intellect's obediential capacity.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3975.summary: Anticipated objection: this contradicts q.1, where Thomas said God cannot be subject of our theology under the absolute, infinite ratio, lest our science equal God's by comprehending all things, creator and creature, created and creatable; here he says the intellect's object includes all these.
claims: Making being as being the intellect's obediential object seems to contradict q.1.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e3995.summary: First reply: the intellect can know all things either all at once — which was denied in q.1, since whoever perfectly comprehends the abyssal ratio of deity knows all things simultaneously and would equal God — or each thing separately as God wills to reveal it, which is what is affirmed here. These do not conflict.
claims: Knowing all things at once is impossible for a creature; knowing each thing in turn by revelation is possible.

HuYgTa-d1e574-d1e4030.summary: Second reply: by common law, creatable things depending on God's free will are not known by any created intellect, but if God reveals them, each is knowable, though not all at once; q.1 is to be understood in the first way, the present claim in the second. This also shows how the first principal argument should be understood. Reply to the argument to the contrary: the major is true, but the minor is false when cognition is taken without love, without which no one is blessed, since vision does not beatify without the will's concurring complacency or its equivalent.
claims: Future contingents depending on God's free will are known only by revelation.
Cognition without love does not beatify.
Vision beatifies only with the will's concurring complacency.

HuYgTa-d1e574-Dd1e5831.summary: Article 4: what the adequate object of our intellect is. Thomas distinguishes the intellect's natural capacity, whose adequate object is phantasiable being (since all natural knowledge derives from the senses), from its obediential capacity, whose adequate object is being as being, including God and all creatable things, since God can reveal himself and anything else. He reconciles this with q.1 by distinguishing simultaneous comprehension of all things (impossible for a creature) from successive knowledge of each thing by revelation, and answers the question's opening arguments: vision without the will's love does not beatify.
claims: The adequate object of the intellect by nature is phantasiable being.
The adequate object of the intellect by obediential potency is being as being.
A creature cannot know all things at once but can know each by revelation.
Vision does not beatify without the will's love.

HuYgTa-d1e574-Dd1e400.summary: Article 3: whether faith and opinion are compossible about the same object. Thomas passes over it, noting that Article 2 already showed their compatibility and that he may return to it in Book 3.
claims: The compatibility of faith and opinion was established in Article 2.

HuYgTa-d1e574-Dd1e329.summary: Article 2: whether the habit of infused faith and the intuitive knowledge of the fatherland can remain together. Thomas affirms that they can, since the lights of faith and glory differ in species and are opposed in none of the modes of opposition. He answers eleven arguments for the incompatibility of faith and science, arguing that contradiction requires the same respect, that faith and opinion are compatible since fear is not of the essence of opinion, that faith is a mean only in a broad sense (unlike Henry's light), and that habits can be perfect and imperfect in different respects. Supporting compatibility with the coexistence of angelic abstractive and intuitive cognition and the confirming role of authority after demonstration, he interprets the authorities to mean that faith ceases in the act of believing but not in its habit — though he defers to Benedict XII's constitution.
claims: Faith and clear vision can coexist.
Faith and science, and faith and opinion, are compatible because they differ in species and respect.
Fear is not of the essence of opinion.
In heaven faith ceases in act but its habit may remain as an adornment of the soul.
Benedict XII's constitution limits what may be held about faith in the blessed.

HuYgTa-d1e574-Dd1e223.summary: Article 1: whether evident knowledge of credibles can be communicated to a wayfarer. Thomas affirms that God can reveal to a wayfarer everything the blessed see, since the intellect is in obediential potency to it, and the person remains a wayfarer if God suspends the will's fruition. He rejects Scotus's restriction of such knowledge to abstractive cognition, answering eight arguments for abstractive knowledge of God and offering seven counter-arguments with rejoinders to a Scotist's replies. His own conclusions are that perfect intuitive knowledge of God is communicable to a wayfarer — supported by arguments from the damned, from miracles, from Christ's vision, from Ambrose and Augustine, and from the separability of accidents in the Eucharist — and that perfect abstractive knowledge of God is impossible. Against Giles of Rome he argues that God can supply the will's intention, and with natural and biblical examples of powers suspended in the presence of their objects he shows that vision without fruition is possible.
claims: God can give a wayfarer intuitive vision of his essence by absolute power.
Such a person remains a wayfarer if the will's fruition is suspended.
Beatitude consists principally in fruition, not vision.
Perfect abstractive knowledge of the divine essence is impossible since no created medium is adequate to it.
God can supply the will's intention for the intellect's act.

HuYgTa-d1e574.summary: Prologue, Question 3: whether evident knowledge of the objects of faith can be communicated to a wayfarer. Thomas holds that by absolute power God can give a wayfarer evident — indeed intuitive — knowledge of everything the blessed see, without his ceasing to be a wayfarer, because beatitude consists essentially in the will's fruition, which God can suspend. Against Scotus he denies that a wayfarer could have perfect abstractive knowledge of the divine essence, which he argues is impossible for any creature. He further holds that the habit of faith can coexist with clear vision and with science and opinion, since their incompatibility is only a matter of the same respect and since fear is not of opinion's essence, though he defers to Benedict XII's constitution on the cessation of acts of faith in the blessed. Finally, he distinguishes the intellect's natural adequate object (phantasiable being) from its obediential adequate object (being as being), reconciling this with q.1.
claims: By absolute power God can give a wayfarer intuitive vision of the divine essence while he remains a wayfarer.
Beatitude consists essentially in fruition, an act of the will that God can suspend.
Perfect abstractive knowledge of the divine essence is impossible.
Faith can coexist with clear vision, science and opinion.
The intellect's natural adequate object is phantasiable being; its obediential object is being as being.
